newsitem.title: UK: Medeva says no sign of key drug competition.
newsitem.headline: Medeva says no sign of key drug competition.

text.p: Britain's Medeva Plc said on Friday that there was no evidence yet of new competition entering the highly-controlled U.S. market for hyperactivity drug Methlyphenidate, its leading product. However, in an interview with Reuters, Medeva chief executive Bill Bogie said he expected Johnson Matthey Plc to start selling its own version of Methylphenidate in the U.S. some time this year. "Two years ago I said it would be two years before they got on to the market. Two years on they are not there yet. There is no sign of them, but I would expect it in the course of this year," Bogie said.

The threat to Methylphenidate, Medeva's main profits engine, has preoccupied analysts. Medeva currently has a 70 percent market share for its generic version of the drug, which is used almost exclusively in the U.S. to control attention deficit disorder in children and young adults.
Because of the sensitive nature of the drug, the U.S. government restricts new entrants tightly, with competitors given an annual sales quota.
Johnson Matthey was granted a licence as a third bulk manufacturer in April 1995, and a number of other companies are known to be interested in the market.
Some analysts now expect competition to be delayed until 1998, which Bogie said would be "very nice."

He added that this would also delay the impact on Medeva's market share, predicting that Johnson Matthey would be granted an initial quota for only 10 to 15 percent of the market. "If competition is delayed until 1998, that clearly is very favourable for us because they will only get a small quota in the first year," Bogie said.
Bogie said prices for the drug had continued to rise this year. Pricing is effectively controlled by Switzerland's Novartis AG, which owns the branded product, Ritalin.

Medeva generally keeps the price of its version 20 percent below Ritalin. Although Bogie said that it was reasonable to think people would have a similar share of the market after four full years of competition, Medeva was optimistic it would eventually regain ground through new formulations of the drug, including a slow-release tablet and a purified version under development by Chiroscince group Plc. "So you can paint a very optimistic picture for Methylphenidate if new (approvals) come through and competition is later than expected," Bogie said. The purified version of the drug would allow lower doses to be administered. It may also have fewer side-effects than existing forms, although this will not become evident until late stage trials have been completed. --Jonathan Birt London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
